The impact of this incident is very unevenly spread.Over 10 years ago, Mozilla shipped OneCRL [1]. We remediated this incident in a couple of hours for Firefox users who were protected automatically without the need for updates. Chrome, Apple and Microsoft have similar tooling. Since then, we've built more advanced tooling to handle revocation at scale for leaf certs (CRLite [2]).However, for the rest of the ecosystem, there has been little to no investment in revocation and for those clients, this is a massive problem. Hopefully, we'll see folks invest now. Efforts like upki [3] look promising.[1] https://blog.mozilla.org/security/2015/03/03/revoking-interm...[2] https://hacks.mozilla.org/2025/08/crlite-fast-private-and-co...[3] https://github.com/rustls/upki

Explanation from eMudhra in the Mozilla bug report https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2083449:> We have done some preliminary assessment, there appears to be a flaw in the KGC script that was used on that specific day to create these ECC issuers. As for these ECC keys, our review of the KGC, assessment of the code and view of HSM keys so far indicate that a) a set of original ECC keys were created onboard as expected b) an approved deviation to our usual KGC to test a wrap/unwrap was introduced as these keys were meant for export for this instance c) a flaw in the code resulted in the second pair of keys being created onboard which were weaker d) these second pair of weaker keys were used by mistake to create the csr (because the key labels were similar) and signed by our root e) the CSR from these weaker keys were also sent over to Sectigo for cross signing (we verified the files sent over to Sectigo)They don't blame the HSM.Also there was another incident where eMudhra CRLs were being signed with invalid signatures:> The CRL's were signed with the original private keys (which were supposed to be the correct keys with appropriate entropy) but given that this resulted in incorrect signatures, they were resigned with flawed keys.

articles.title: Tsrs: A Port of TypeScript to Rust
articles.summary: Tsrs: A Port of TypeScript to Rust

top_comments: Hey there, TypeScript team member here. The tsrs project has been extremely interesting to see come together. We've been working with the maintainers to better understand how tsrs is fast and what sorts of optimizations it uses are safe. We even did our own Rust vibe port and what we currently suspect is that a lot of the speed does not just come down to language choice, and some of what is going to make TS 7.1 faster and leaner (see the charts in the blog post) actually comes from optimizations discovered in tsrs.We think the wasm and oxlint integration makes a lot of sense for Cloudflare's needs, so this investment makes sense. At the same time, we'll be working hard and collaborating to make the official TypeScript toolset faster and even more efficient.Congrats to the tsrs team on making this official. We're excited and we look forward to continuing on collaboration!

It appears they're using a unique memory model (https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/docs/PORTING.m...) to overcome the challenge that prevented the TypeScript team from choosing Rust to begin with: Rust has no GC and porting from a GC language to it often requires restructure of data.Essentially, they fake a GC via never-freed arenas for long-living objects. It's interesting that Rust can do that (hopefully soundly)!

Ah took me a while to understand the reason behind this.It wasn’t “let’s build a faster Rust based Typescript compiler” at all. That was a nice side-effect.They needed a Typescript compiler that can run on their WASM only sandbox. So the only existing option was to export tsc Go to WASM, but that comes with the full Go runtime.And to avoid that cost, they experimented with a Rust compiler and turns out it’s even faster than the reference tsc/Go implementation.

articles.title: What shall I teach my son?
articles.summary: What shall I teach my son?

top_comments: My mum was a mechanic, my dad was a mechanic/truck driver.My grandfather and uncle were mechanics...I am not, in fact my understanding of mechanics is extremely basic.If I go back into my family tree, I can find three generations of Sugar House Labourers in Scotland in the early 1800s.. a profession that no longer exists in the UK as far as I can tell, and I'm certain they had a specialisation.We'll be fine, your children aren't you, they'll find their own passions.Our jobs as parents is to teach values and make sure they're good people and have the tools to make good decisions too, not to set them on a particular path... that's a losing goal, we can't tell the future for the next year- how could we possibly predict what works well 20 years from now?

> My wife and I are expecting our first child.> I once tried to come up with a single-word purpose for education, and I landed upon the word “resourceful” ...As someone who's a little further ahead in this process, I realized the true raison d'etre for education might actually not be any of the reason discussed..It's so you, the children's parents, can go about your business for the day and the kids can stay somewhere safe and where they can interact with their peers. If they happened to learn something, that's pure bonus.
